title: CCDV-F Mock Exam #16 (Moderate Tier)
description: Full-length 53-question moderate-difficulty simulation for Claude Certified Developer - Foundations (120 minutes). Realistic exam-style mix of easier, medium, and hard scenario questions.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team budgets a summarization feature with a rule of thumb of about four characters per token, measured on the model they ran last year. After moving to a newer model generation, the bill rises roughly 15% on identical documents. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Newer models bill input by character length rather than by token, since longer documents cost proportionally more regardless of how they are tokenized.
The old rule is stale; characters per token depends on the tokenizer, which differs by generation, so count tokens on every new model.
The old rule only affects estimates of response length; input is tokenized identically across generations, so the extra cost came from longer outputs.
Tokens map to a fixed number of characters on every Claude model, so the increase must come from a higher per-token price on the newer tier.

questions.explanation: Claude counts tokens, not characters or words, and the average number of characters per token depends on the tokenizer of the model in use, which differs between model generations. A rule of thumb measured on one model should not be carried to another. Re-measure token counts on the model you actually deploy, and confirm tokenizer behavior again whenever the model changes.

distractor_explanations.A: Tokens are the unit of both pricing and budget on every model. Billing is not done in characters or words.
distractor_explanations.C: Tokenization of the input changes between generations as well. The rule of thumb is model-dependent for input and output alike.
distractor_explanations.D: Characters per token is not constant. It varies with the tokenizer of each model generation, so identical text can produce a different token count.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A summarizer's test suite checks that each response is valid JSON with a non-empty `actions` array, and it passes on every run. The team now also wants to know whether each summary is faithful to the source thread. Which approach fits?

options.text: Add an eval with a model-graded judge and a faithfulness rubric, and keep all the structural checks as property assertions.
Set temperature to 0 and compare the response text with a stored copy, which makes an exact comparison dependable for faithfulness.
Extend the structural checks with more required fields, because a response that parses and carries every field must also be faithful.
Assert that each response exactly matches a stored reference summary, so any difference in wording is flagged as a regression.

questions.explanation: Because sampling makes output non-deterministic, tests should assert on properties that must hold, such as a field being present or the structure parsing. Judging meaning, for example whether a summary is faithful, is a different job that structure checks cannot do, so an eval with a model-graded judge and a clear rubric is the right tool for that part.

distractor_explanations.B: Temperature 0 makes output more repeatable but never guarantees identical text. Also, the newest models reject non-default sampling values.
distractor_explanations.C: Structure checks show that a response is well formed. They say nothing about whether its content is faithful to the source.
distractor_explanations.D: Identical inputs do not guarantee identical outputs, and the same correct answer can be worded many ways, so exact-text assertions fail inconsistently.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A developer includes three worked examples in the first request so Claude will learn the required output format, then drops them from later requests to save tokens. Later responses drift back to the old format. Why?

options.text: Three samples were too few for the format to stick; roughly ten examples are needed before the model keeps the pattern in later requests.
Sampling randomness overrode the earlier examples, so lowering the temperature would have kept the format stable in the later requests.
The API caches the examples per conversation, and the format fades once the default cache lifetime ends, so they have to be added again.
Examples work only while they are in the prompt, because they are not training data, so they must accompany every call that needs them.

questions.explanation: Zero-shot, one-shot, and multi-shot describe how many worked examples sit in the prompt. The examples are not training data: they show the model the shape of the answer only for the request that contains them. If a later call needs the format, the examples have to be in that call, which is also why each example costs tokens on every request.

distractor_explanations.A: Examples are not training data at any count. They influence a response only while they are present in the prompt.
distractor_explanations.B: The examples were no longer in the prompt, so there was nothing for the model to follow. Temperature does not restore removed context.
distractor_explanations.C: Caching is a cost and latency mechanism for repeated prefixes. It does not act as memory of examples from earlier requests.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A support engineer pastes one screenshot of a UI bug into an internal tool, which sends it with a question and waits for the answer. The image is never reused. A teammate proposes adding a Files API upload step first. What is the better call?

options.text: Submit it through the Message Batches API, which lowers the per-token cost of each request that carries an image, interactive or not.
Host the image at a short-lived signed URL and pass that, so Claude fetches it when the request runs and no bytes travel inline.
Upload through the Files API anyway, because a `file_id` always reduces the number of visual tokens charged for the image.
Send it inline as base64 in the message; a one-off image gains nothing from an extra upload step to the Files API.

questions.explanation: Inline base64 is best for a one-off image where an upload step would add complexity without a payoff. The Files API pays off when the same asset appears in many requests, and a URL source needs a stable public address. Batch is for offline workloads, not for a person who is waiting.

distractor_explanations.A: Batch suits offline work. Here a person is waiting on an immediate answer, so the added latency is unacceptable.
distractor_explanations.B: URL references need a stable, public, reachable address. A short-lived signed link is the case to avoid.
distractor_explanations.C: A `file_id` removes payload weight from later requests. It does not change the visual token cost, and a single use gets no benefit.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A service sends 1,120 × 840 pixel page images to Claude, one visual token per 28 × 28 pixel patch, with no downscaling. A request may spend at most 20,000 visual tokens on images. How many such images can one request carry?

options.text: 285 images, found by adding the two patch counts (40 + 30) to get 70 visual tokens per image and dividing 20,000 by that.
500 images, found by counting only the 40 patches across the width of each image and ignoring the 30 rows down its height.
17 images, since 20,000 / 1,200 is about 16.7, and a fraction of an image still rounds up to a full one.
16 images, because each costs 40 × 30 = 1,200 visual tokens and 20,000 / 1,200 is about 16.7.

questions.explanation: An image costs ⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉ visual tokens. Here 1,120 / 28 = 40 and 840 / 28 = 30, so each page image costs 40 × 30 = 1,200 tokens. Twenty thousand divided by 1,200 is about 16.7, and since a partial image cannot be sent, 16 images fit; a seventeenth would reach 20,400 tokens. Adding the patch counts or counting only one dimension gives far larger, wrong capacities.

distractor_explanations.A: The patches form a grid, so the counts are multiplied, giving 1,200 tokens per image rather than 70.
distractor_explanations.B: Both dimensions count. Each image spans 40 patches across and 30 down, which is 1,200 tokens, not 40.
distractor_explanations.C: A seventeenth image would push the request to 20,400 tokens, over the limit, so only whole images that fit can be counted.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team estimates the cost of a 6,000 × 4,000 pixel photo by applying ⌈w / 28⌉ × ⌈h / 28⌉ to the original size and gets a very large number. The model's documented image limits are far smaller than that photo. How should they estimate the cost?

options.text: Keep the original-size figure, since the API charges visual tokens on the uploaded pixels and shrinks the image only for display.
Apply the formula to the scaled size, because oversized images are downscaled first; confirm limits at build time.
Treat the model's visual-token limit as the cost of each image, with larger images simply rejected by the API instead of being resized.
Send it through the Files API, which resizes each uploaded image to one standard size, so each image costs the same number of tokens.

questions.explanation: Each model has a maximum native image resolution, given as a long-edge limit and a visual-token limit, and an image above either limit is downscaled before processing. The patch formula therefore runs on the scaled dimensions. Analogy: a mail slot only takes envelopes up to a set size, so a poster mailed through it is folded down first, and the postage is charged on the folded package rather than on the flat poster. The photo is the poster, the model's limits are the slot, and visual tokens are the postage. Using the original size overstates the cost, and the limits differ by model tier and change over time, so confirm them at build time.

distractor_explanations.A: Images above the limits are downscaled before processing, so the formula runs on the scaled dimensions, not the uploaded ones.
distractor_explanations.C: Oversized images are downscaled rather than rejected, and smaller images cost less than the limit.
distractor_explanations.D: The Files API changes how an image is sent. It does not set a standard size or a fixed token cost.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A pipeline attaches several high-resolution photos to each request and runs past its token budget once real volume arrives. What is the most direct first fix?

options.text: Move the photos into the system prompt, where input tokens are counted at a lower rate than they are in the user turn of a request.
Send the job through the Message Batches API, which keeps the images out of the context window during processing.
Add a resize step that shrinks images before sending, after measuring a typical production image against the context limit.
Recompress each photo as a smaller JPEG file, which lowers the visual-token count along with the number of encoded bytes.

questions.explanation: Images are charged in visual tokens, ⌈width / 28⌉ × ⌈height / 28⌉ per image, so cost follows pixel dimensions rather than file size. The fix for an over-budget image pipeline is often a short resize step. It is far cheaper to find the problem before deployment, by measuring a typical production image against the context limit before writing the ingestion code.

distractor_explanations.A: Every block in the request counts toward the budget in the same way, wherever it sits in the request.
distractor_explanations.B: Batches change the price and when results arrive, not how many visual tokens each image uses.
distractor_explanations.D: Visual tokens come from pixel dimensions in 28 by 28 patches, so a smaller file with the same dimensions costs the same.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team maps the work on a Claude application onto the systems lifecycle. Which TWO activities belong in the test phase? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Writing an integration check that passes real retrieval output into the prompt builder and the model call.
Running the eval suite against the graded cases and reading the per-case results to see what failed.
Instrumenting token cost, latency, and error rate for each call once the system is live in production.
Pinning the full model ID and keeping the prior version available as a rollback target ahead of the release.
Choosing the platform that satisfies the customer's residency requirement before the building work starts.

questions.explanation: The lifecycle runs requirements, design, build, test, deploy, operate, and iterate. The test phase is where the built system is checked: evals against graded cases, plus unit, integration, and end-to-end checks that each catch a different kind of break. Pinning a version is deploy work, choosing the platform is design work, and instrumenting live traffic is operate work. Analogy: before a new bridge opens, inspectors load-test each span and check that the spans meet cleanly at the joints. That inspection day is the test phase, while picking the river crossing was design, hanging the opening-day signs is deploy, and counting traffic afterward is operate.

distractor_explanations.C: Instrumenting live traffic belongs to the operate phase, after release.
distractor_explanations.D: Pinning a version and keeping a rollback target is deploy-phase work, not a test activity.
distractor_explanations.E: Choosing the platform and its constraints is design-phase work. Test checks a built system.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A partner wants to embed an agent in its own product, with iteration, tool execution, observation, and termination handled for it, much as Claude Code does in a terminal. Which package provides that loop?

options.text: The Claude Agent SDK, which exposes the same agent loop that powers Claude Code and can be embedded inside a product.
The async client in the Anthropic SDK, where non-blocking calls let the model plan and run its own follow-up steps.
A raw REST client, where the endpoint itself runs the tool-execution loop and returns just the final answer to the caller.
Claude Managed Agents, installed as a library so that the hosted loop and its sandbox run inside the partner's own process.

questions.explanation: The Claude Agent SDK gives programmatic access to the same agent loop that powers Claude Code: iteration, tool execution, observation, and termination. That lets a partner embed an agent in its own product instead of running Claude Code in a terminal. It is distinct from the Anthropic SDK, which is a thin convenience wrapper over the API and does not run an agent loop. Neither an async client nor a raw REST call adds a loop.

distractor_explanations.B: Async calls avoid blocking the application's thread. They add no agent behavior.
distractor_explanations.C: The REST endpoint returns one response per request. Looping over tool calls is left to the caller's code or to an SDK that provides it.
distractor_explanations.D: Managed Agents is the path where Anthropic runs the loop and the sandbox; the application streams events to it rather than running it in-process.
